Three glass beakers side-by-side. 1: "Unsaturated solution": a small spoon of blue copper(II) tetraoxosulphate(VI) crystals dissolving completely into a clear pale blue liquid. 2: "Saturated solution": a darker blue liquid with a pile of undissolved blue crystals resting on the bottom. 3: "Supersaturated solution": a very dark blue liquid with a single large seed crystal dropped in, triggering rapid crystal growth radiating outward.

A line graph titled "Solubility Curves". The y-axis is "Solubility (mol dm⁻³)" and the x-axis is "Temperature (°C)". It shows three curves: a steep upward curve for KNO₃ showing solubility rising rapidly with temperature, a very flat nearly horizontal line for NaCl showing solubility barely changing, and a downward-sloping curve for a gas or Ca(OH)₂.

Three glass beakers side-by-side in a dark room. A flashlight shines a beam from the left through all three. The first beaker (True Solution, like salt water) shows no visible beam inside the clear liquid. The second beaker (Colloid, like dilute milk) shows a distinct, glowing solid beam of light passing through the slightly cloudy liquid (Tyndall effect). The third beaker (Suspension, like muddy water) shows a cloudy liquid with large particles settling at the bottom, heavily blocking and scattering the light randomly. Clean flat textbook style.
